title: Quality Engineering
blurb: Build confidence with testing that actually catches bugs. It's not just about making the coverage numbers beautiful.

mustKnow.title: Test pyramid and when should the shape change?
mustKnow.body: Mike Cohn's idea is to have lots of unit tests at the base because they're fast and accurate at pinpointing failures, integration tests in the middle, and a few E2E tests at the top for important flows because they're slow and brittle. But this proportion is not a fixed rule. If most of the code is connected to a database or other service, bugs often lie in the connections. Therefore, more weight should be given to the integration test (Kent C. Dodds called this shape the testing trophy). A rule of thumb is always to test each risk at the lowest layer that actually captures it. And watch out for ice cream cones that have E2E or manual tests rather than unit tests.

mustKnow.title: Good unit tests: AAA and one behavior per test.
mustKnow.body: Divide tests into Arrange (prepare data), Act (call things to be tested) and Assert (check results). Let each test examine a single behavior and name it with conditions and expected results. When it fails, you will immediately know which behavior is broken without having to read the code. One behavior does not mean that you cannot have multiple expect lines. If every line checks for the same result, such as different fields of the returned object, and good tests must run independently of each other. It does not rely on the sequence or state that other tests leave behind.

mustKnow.title: Test behavior, not implementation.
mustKnow.body: Tests should ask what is put in and what comes out through the public interface, not how many times internal methods are called or in what order. Tests tied to internal details will break every time you refactor them, even if the behavior doesn't change. Teams will start to shy away from refactoring or fixing tests in the code until it no longer catches bugs. A common warning sign is having to export internal functions just to test them.

mustKnow.title: Test double: mock, stub and fake
mustKnow.body: All are representations of things that are slow or uncontrollable, such as a network, timer, or payment gateway. A stub returns a predefined value. A fake is an abbreviated version of something that actually works, such as a repository that stores data in memory. A mock is used to check that it is being called with the correct data. Suitable for side effects that cannot be seen from the results, such as sending an email. In Jest, all models are usually created with jest.fn() and are called mock, but separating roles helps to make the right decision whether to check the result or check the call.

mustKnow.title: Boundary value: Bugs like to live at the edges.
mustKnow.body: Mistakes like using > instead of >= or off-by-one in loops are more likely to escape if you only test neutral values, because many models only show values ​​on the edges of the condition. Divide the input into equivalence partitions and test for edge values ​​on both sides. For example, the free pass rule from 500 should test 499 and 500, not 100 and 1000. And don't forget edges that are often overlooked, such as negative 0s, empty lists, empty strings, and null.

mustKnow.title: Linter, formatter and static analysis
mustKnow.body: Tools that check code without having to run it, such as ESLint, TypeScript's type checker, and formatters like Prettier, can detect the same types of problems throughout the code, such as unused variables with mismatched types or promises that are forgotten to await (via Typescript-eslint rules), faster and cheaper than writing individual tests. Run the same results across editors, pre-commits, and CIs so that reviewers focus on logic and design instead of discussing style. But these tools do not know whether the business rules are correct or not, so they cannot be used as a substitute for testing.

mustKnow.title: What does Code coverage say and what does it not say?
mustKnow.body: Coverage tells which lines or branches were run during a test, so it's useful for finding code that hasn't been tested yet. But it doesn't say that the results are checked. Tests that call functions without expectation can increase coverage. Setting numbers as a mandatory target often results in meaningless tests. Use coverage (especially branch coverage) to find blind spots. It's not to prove that the test is good.

mustKnow.title: Flaky test: Some pass, some fail.
mustKnow.body: test with uncertain results even though the code has not changed This is often due to dependencies on real time, sleep waits, shared state execution sequences between tests or external networks. The biggest danger is that teams get so used to pressing rerun that they overlook red flags that are actually bugs. Fix the root cause, such as using fake timers or sending in clocks and separating the state of each test. If you can't fix it immediately, quarantine it with follow-up work, not put it in a permanent retry.

mustKnow.title: TDD: Red, Green, Refactor
mustKnow.body: Write tests that fail for the next behavior first (Red). Write as little code as possible to pass (Green). Then make the code clean with tests to protect it (Refactor). Seeing a test fail first proves that the test actually checks what it intended. If it passes from the beginning, it means the test is probably wrong or the behavior already exists. TDD is suitable for logic with clear rules and quick feedback. For survey work or UI that still changes frequently, tests may be written after it.

mustKnow.title: Over-mocking: test is green but the system is broken.
mustKnow.body: When mocking every dependency, including our own classes, the test only checks to see if the code is calling what we think is correct. If the mock returns a value that the real thing never returns, such as incorrect SQL or a renamed field, the test is still green. This is a sign that the mock's setup is longer than the test itself, or the test breaks every time we refactor the mock only to an edge system that we don't own. Use fake when possible and have integration tests with the real thing, such as using Testcontainers to run the real database in a container.

mustKnow.title: Performance and load testing
mustKnow.body: Measure how the system responds under load, such as a load test that loads as expected, a stress test that pushes to the limit to find limits, and a long soak test to find memory leaks. Look at high percentile latencies (p95, p99) along with error rates instead of averages, because the average covers up very slow users. Results are meaningful when the environment, data volume, and usage patterns are close to real. Widely used tools include k6, JMeter, Gatling and Locust.

mustKnow.title: Contract testing and mutation testing
mustKnow.body: Contract testing checks that the consumer and provider still talk to each other in a consumer-driven way (e.g. Pact). The consumer records what they expect from the API into a contract and the provider's CI checks it every time. So it can catch field changes without having to have E2E across every service. Mutation testing (such as StrykerJS for JavaScript or PIT for Java) modifies the code one point at a time, such as changing >= to > and then runs a test. If the test still passes (mutant survived), this usually means there is no test to actually detect that behavior (except for equivalent mutants that produce the same results as the original code, with no tests that can be separated). This is a measure of test quality that is more accurate than coverage, but runs slowly, so it is often run only on changed code or in cycles.

mustKnow.title: ISTQB's 7 Testing Principles
mustKnow.body: There are 7 general principles that can be applied to all types of testing: testing can show that a defect exists but cannot prove that it doesn't exist. You cannot test everything so you have to choose techniques and risks. Starting testing at an early stage reduces time and costs. Defects tend to be concentrated in a few components. Tests that are repeated until used are less likely to catch new defects (tests wear out). Tests and data must be adjusted. Testing methods depend on the context. Repeating is not useful. Even though the document states that rerunning some cases, such as automated regression, still gives good results.

mustKnow.title: What is the difference between test level and test type?
mustKnow.body: test level is "test at which layer of the system" which ISTQB divides into component (or unit), component integration, system, system integration and acceptance. Test type is "what is tested" such as functional, non-functional (performance, security, usability, etc.), black-box and white-box. Each type can be done at every level, for example, measuring the response time of a single function is non-functional test at component level A common trap is confusing component integration (joints between components within the system) with system integration (connections with other systems or external services, such as a payment gateway).

mustKnow.title: Confirmation testing and regression testing
mustKnow.body: After debugging, two different things need to be done: confirmation testing to check that the original defect has actually been fixed (i.e. rerun the previously failed case), and regression testing to check that the changes Including making changes that have already been confirmed does not break other parts, whether in the original component, other components, or connected systems. For example, fixing a coupon formula and running it in the case of a coupon that was previously incorrect. (confirmation) and run a checkout test with the entire set of prices (regression). Because the regression suite is run frequently and continues to grow, it is suitable for automate and run in CI, and impact analysis should be done to determine the scope of which parts should be run.

mustKnow.title: Testing async code: must await or return promise
mustKnow.body: Jest needs to know when the code is finished, so it must return a promise or use async/await. If you forget, the test will end before the promise resolves or rejects, and the result is unreliable. You can use .resolves and .rejects when you want readability, but you must always await or return. If you choose to write try/catch, you must cause the test to fail when the promise is fulfilled (not throw), such as putting expect.assertions(n) or storing errors in a variable and expecting outside of catch, because otherwise the test will pass without ever checking anything.

mustKnow.title: Setup/teardown and state separation between tests
mustKnow.body: beforeEach and afterEach run every test cycle, beforeAll and afterAll run only once per file or per describe hook. The describe hook affects only the tests in that block, and the top-level beforeEach runs before the underlying beforeEach. A classic symptom is that a test passes when run alone (test.only) but fails when run as a whole. This means there is state that other tests left behind. Create or reset the data in beforeEach instead of creating an editable object at the file level or in beforeAll and then share it.

mustKnow.title: Good Defect report: severity and priority
mustKnow.body: A defect report is for people to duplicate and fix without having to ask, so it should have a short title, test object and environment, steps that led to it, expected result versus actual result, log or screenshot, severity, priority, and status. ISTQB's syllabus defines severity as the degree of impact on the stakeholder or the requirement, and priority as "priority to fix" or the order of fixes. In practice, these two values ​​do not have to go the same way, such as the distorted logo on the home page before tomorrow's press conference. It has little impact on work but should be fixed immediately.

mustKnow.title: Decision table and state transition testing
mustKnow.body: A decision table is used with rules whose results depend on a combination of conditions. The rows are the conditions and actions, the columns are the individual rules, and coverage is the proportion of possible columns that the test covers, helping to spot missing combinations or conflicting rules. But the number of rules grows quickly with the number of conditions (3 true/false conditions, 8 combinations). State transition testing is used for systems whose behavior depends on states, such as orders. A test case is a sequence of events that take the system to change state, and the coverage that the syllabus brings up is three levels: all states, valid transitions, and all transitions. The latter must try to make invalid transitions as well, trying one test at a time so that one defect doesn't cover the other.

mustKnow.title: E2E with Playwright: locator, auto-wait and web-first assertion
mustKnow.body: Playwright waits for the element to be ready before doing it himself. (auto-waiting) For example, before clicking, it will check that the element is a single element, visible, still, not blocked and enabled, so you don't have to set sleep yourself. Choose the locator as the user sees, such as getByRole instead of CSS or XPath that is tied to the DOM structure and use web-first assertions like await expect(locator).toBeVisible() which retry until the condition is true. But if you write expect(await locator.isVisible()).toBe(true) It checks only once and ends immediately, making the test flaky. In addition, each test should be run independently, not relying on the state of the previous test.

mustKnow.title: Snapshot testing: Use it correctly and give real reviews.
mustKnow.body: snapshot test collects serialized values ​​and puts them in a text file And the next round is compared with diff, so it's suitable for small results that need to check the specific structure, such as the output of a component or an error message. The .snap file must be treated as part of the test, which is to commit it to the repo and look at the diff when reviewing it. And values ​​that change every time, such as time and random id, must be controlled. If you use deterministic or use the property matcher on CI, Jest won't write a new snapshot for you. If you press jest -u to make it green without reading what's changed, the test will become a rubber stamp that approves everything.

mustKnow.title: Property-based testing with fast-check
mustKnow.body: Instead of choosing a sample value yourself, write a property that is the relationship between input and output that must be true for every input value. Then the library will randomly generate a large number of inputs, and when it finds incorrect cases it will try to shrink it to a counterexample. As small as possible. An example property that comes to mind is that the sorting result must not decrease and remain the same length, or decode(encode(x)) must return x. General precautions (not from this page) is a property that is recalculated using the same formula as the code. will be wrong all at once and not catch anything

mustKnow.title: Risk-based testing: Ranking according to risk.
mustKnow.body: When it is not possible to test everything, ISTQB recommends selecting and ranking tests based on risk. Risk level is derived from likelihood (chance of occurrence) and impact (impact), which is quantitatively assessed by multiplying them together. or qualitative risk matrix results are used to determine test level and technique scope and depth of coverage. For example, newly written authentication code should be tested more heavily than renaming button labels, and defect locations are also inputs to the evaluation.

mustKnow.title: jest.mock is hoist and partial mock
mustKnow.body: When using babel-jest, the jest.mock command will be raised to the top of the file before import, so variables declared above cannot be referenced. Jest will error that factory does not reference variables outside of scope, except for variables whose names start with mock, which the author must guarantee that they are configured in time. If you mock a module with factory that only returns some exports, the rest will be lost. Use jest.requireActual. Keep the real stuff and replace only the desired ones (partial mock). And if you want different mocks in each test, use jest.doMock that is not hoisted.

questions.prompt: Almost all services receive requests and read and write PostgreSQL. There are many unit tests that all mock repositories, but almost all production bugs come from incorrect SQL and migrations that don't match the code. How should I adjust my testing strategy?
options: Add unit tests to the mock repository to cover all types of queries.
Add an integration test that runs with real PostgreSQL, such as in a container.
Write E2E through the UI for every case of every endpoint.
Set a minimum coverage of 90% in CI for every PR to pass.
questions.explain: The bug is at the junction with the database, which is invisible to the mock. Therefore, more weight should be given to integration tests, which is the lowest layer that catches this bug. Adding unit tests to the mock repository will cause the test to continue to run green even if the SQL is incorrect. E2E in all cases is unnecessarily slow and brittle.

questions.prompt: This test fails in CI and only reports that the “order” is broken. What is the main problem with this test?
options: There are many expect lines. A good unit test must always have one expect.
Create a real Order instead of a mock, so it is not counted as a unit test.
Combine many behaviors into one test. When it breaks, you don't know which behavior is broken.
Not using beforeEach to prepare data, making the test difficult to read and slow.
questions.explain: This test checks billing, coupons, and cancellations under one name. When it breaks, you must read the code and expect after the point of failure will not be run at all. It should be separated into tests and behaviors with names that tell the expected results. As for having multiple lines of expect, it's not wrong if every line checks for the same behavior.

questions.prompt: This test always passes on the developer machine, but fails on CI sometimes when the machine is under heavy load. How should I solve it?
options: Increase sleep to 2000 ms to allow enough time on slow CI machines.
Set CI to retry tests that fail automatically 3 times before reporting results.
Let startReportJob return promise and await instead of guessing the time with sleep.
Move this test to run last to prevent other tests from competing for CPU.
questions.explain: test relies on the assumption that the job will be completed in 200 ms, which is unrealistic on slow machines. Waiting for the desired event directly (Or control the time with fake timers) so fix the root cause. Adding sleep only reduces the chance of failure but makes the test suite slower every time. Retry hides the problem.

questions.prompt: You do TDD to add the rule “VIP members get 10% discount”. Write a new test and run it. It passes immediately even though you haven't edited the code yet. What should I do next?
options: Good, you can skip to the refactor step because test is now green.
Delete this test because tests that never fail are useless.
Continue writing the discount code as planned. Then come back and look at the test later.
Check test first because it may not detect new behavior. Or does this rule already exist?
questions.explain: The Red step is to prove that test catches the lack of this behavior. If the test passes from the beginning, the test may assert incorrectly, for example, the customer was not set to VIP or the code already has this rule. Skipping to refactor risks creating a test that is not immune to redemption.

questions.prompt: The refactor team rounds the penny only once at the end. The amount of money that the customer sees remains the same in every case, but this test fails. What should I do?
options: Change the number in toHaveBeenCalledTimes to 1 to match the new code.
Changed to assert total returned by checkout instead of call count.
Roll back the refactor because a failed test means the behavior has changed.
mock roundToSatang Return the constant value test so it doesn't depend on rounding.
questions.explain: This test is tied to internal calculation methods. So it breaks even though the results don't change. Changing the number to 1 actually makes it pass, but it's still brittle and will break again in the next refactor. You should check the results that the user sees, such as expect(checkout(cart).total).toBe(...)

questions.prompt: The ticketing system offers student prices to those ages 13–19 (13 and 19 combined). Which age set best tests this rule?
options: 15 is the only value because it is in the middle of the range and is representative.
1, 15, 50 and 99 to distribute to all age groups.
12, 13, 19, and 20 are the values ​​on both sides of the range.
13 and 19 because they are values ​​written in the requirements
questions.explain: < and <= or off-by-one bugs appear on the edge, so you need to test both the values ​​within and outside the range on both sides of the edge. Sets 13 and 19 only test the inside side. If the code is incorrectly written as age <= 20, it still passes.

questions.prompt: Most of the comments in the team's PR were about spacing, import order, and variables that were declared but not used, so much so that logic was less discussed. How should I solve it?
options: Write a detailed style guide and have reviewers help enforce it.
Set formatter and linter to run automatically in editor, pre-commit and CI.
Added unit tests that check the coding style of each file.
Let one senior reviewer make all style decisions.
questions.explain: Work that can be checked by rules should be done by a machine. Because it's consistent, you don't forget, and you can fix it automatically. Reviewers can therefore concentrate on logic and design. The style guide that is given to reviewers still takes the same amount of time to review and each person can interpret it differently.

questions.prompt: Coverage of this function is 100%, but mutation testing reports that mutants changed >= to > survived. What does that mean?
options: There is no test that can separate >= and > from each other. Should be increased in the case of total 500.
The tool is set incorrectly because coverage 100% means the test is complete.
The code should be changed to > according to mutant because the test still passes.
You need to add several more test values ​​in the range 100 to 1000 to make it denser.
questions.explain: The mutant survived, meaning that the code has been fixed and the test still passes, so there is no test to check the behavior at the edge of 500. Increasing the median value doesn't help because >= and > give different results only at 500. This is something coverage cannot tell.

questions.prompt: service Orders calls the API of service Users that another team maintains. The Users team changes the field name from fullName to name and then deploys it. Both teams' tests pass, but the Orders break in production. What is the most effective way to prevent this problem?
options: Let Orders mock Users' responses in more detail in unit tests.
Add unit tests on the users side until coverage reaches 100% before deploying.
Conduct consumer-driven contract tests where Users' CIs are checked against Orders' contracts.
Have every team run E2E across every service in staging before every deployment.
questions.explain: Mock on the Orders side is written from the Orders' own understanding, so it stays green even if users change contract tests, allowing consumer expectations to be checked in the provider's CI and caught before deploying. E2E across all services can be caught, but is slow, brittle, and relies on staging that all teams use together.

questions.prompt: Load testing of the product search API achieved an average latency of 120 ms, which exceeded the target, but some users complained that searches were sometimes very slow. What should I watch next?
options: latency at p95 and p99 and error rate under the same load
Rerun the load test with a reduced number of simulated users to make the results more stable.
The median value is because it tolerates outliers better than the average.
It is considered passing because the average is within the target. Users who complain probably have slow internet.
questions.explain: Both the average and median cancel out the group of very slow requests. If p99 is several seconds, 1 out of 100 requests will wait that long even though the average looks good, so high percentiles and error rates need to be looked at together. Reducing the load makes the results look better but doesn't match the actual conditions.

questions.prompt: A set of 600 automatic regression tests ran every night for half a year. But features that the team fixes frequently still have new bugs leaking to users. Which conclusion is most consistent with the testing principles?
options: The original test set caught fewer new defects. Tests and data should be adjusted according to the changed parts.
Green every night means there are no defects left. The bug that was released is a changed requirement, not the fault of the test.
Automatic regression should be stopped entirely because running the same test over and over has no value.
You should run the same set of tests more often, several times per night, to catch more bugs.
questions.explain: The "tests wear out" principle states that repeated tests will catch fewer new defects, so tests and data must be adjusted or written more. But the documentation indicates that reruns are still useful in some cases, such as automated regression, so they are not deprecated. As for running more frequently, it doesn't help because the same test set still checks the same things.

questions.prompt: Based on several months of defect history, most of the bugs reported by customers were in a single tax calculation module. Before release, the team had limited testing time. How should I allocate my time?
options: Time is divided equally across modules so that it is fair and no part is left out.
Specially increase the testing time at the tax calculation module because defects tend to be concentrated.
Skip the tax module and test the other modules first. Because there are many bugs, it means that testing will never end.
Test only newly written modules. because the old module has been used
questions.explain: The defects cluster principle states that a small number of components often have the majority of defects, and old defect information is the input to risk-based sequencing. So you should invest there. Equal division appears fair but is not associated with risk. As for skipping it because there are a lot of bugs, it's the opposite of principle.

questions.prompt: The team tested all requirements in the spec and fixed all found bugs. But after the release, users complained that the steps didn't match their actual work and were too difficult to use. This situation corresponds to which idea?
options: Pesticide paradox: Rerun of the same test cannot detect new defects anymore.
Exhaustive testing is impossible: not every possible input and path can be tested.
Absence-of-defects fallacy: Passing all requirements does not mean meeting the user's needs.
Defect clustering: All bugs are clustered together in a single module of the system.
questions.explain: Checking that the system complies with the spec (verification) does not guarantee that the spec meets actual needs, so it must be validated, such as having real users try it or doing acceptance testing. The pesticide paradox refers to the effectiveness of repeated tests, which is not a problem in this case.

questions.prompt: The team writes tests that call the payment gateway of the external service provider in the sandbox to check that the requests and responses are as agreed upon. According to ISTQB's classification, what test level is it classified as?
options: Component testing to directly test our payment modules in isolation
Component integration testing: tests the connections between two pieces of code.
Acceptance testing because it uses data that is close to the real thing in testing.
System integration testing because it tests connections with external services.
questions.explain: System integration testing focuses on the connections between the system being tested and other systems and external services, and should be done in a near-real environment. Component integration addresses the connections between components within the same system. This is the most confusing choice.

questions.prompt: Dev fixes the bug of overlapping discount coupons that charge the wrong amount. QA runs the same case that failed and passed. Before closing the ticket, what should be done according to testing principles?
options: Run a regression test on areas that might be affected, such as price and checkout.
You can close the ticket now because confirmation testing has passed which means the resolution is complete.
Run the same case again dozens of times. Until you're sure it's not flaky before turning it off.
Test only the screen showing the discount. Because the user sees the results there and does not need to look at other parts.
questions.explain: Confirmation testing only checks to see if the original bug has been fixed. Regression testing checks to make sure the change doesn't cause any other negative effects. This must be done even if the correction has been made through confirmation. The option to close immediately is missed here.

questions.prompt: In e-commerce systems, which bug can be described as "low serverity, high priority"?
options: The payment page crashes every time a customer uses a credit card during a flash sale, causing the sale to fail.
Export feature for old reports that no one has enabled. Causes the entire system to crash when a button is pressed.
The brand's name is misspelled on the campaign page launching tomorrow morning. The system still works normally.
The language switch button is misaligned by two pixels on some phones, which hardly anyone notices.
questions.explain: Severity is the level of impact, while priority is the urgency of the solution. which do not need to be consistent The wrong brand name has low systemic impact but must be corrected before launch. On the payment front, both values ​​are high. And the fact that a feature that no one uses causes the entire system to crash means that the severity is high but the priority is low because there are hardly any users who encounter it.

questions.prompt: Shipping cost rules: Customers have 3 true/false conditions: being a member, reaching the threshold, and having a free shipping coupon. The results of each combination are different. If a full decision table is created and nothing has been removed, how many rules are there and how is coverage measured?
options: 3 rules, one rule, one condition and measured by the number of conditions that are fully tested
8 rules and measured by the proportion of possible rules that are covered by test.
6 rules because each condition has two values. and measured by the total number of tests
9 rules of three conditions multiplied by three values and measured by lines of code that are executed
questions.explain: The three true/false conditions give 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combinations, and the coverage of the decision table is the number of possible columns that are tested. Divide by the total number of possible columns. Thinking additively or one rule per condition makes a mistake. Because the results depend on the combination of conditions.

questions.prompt: Orders have statuses: Created, Paid, Shipped, Closed, and can only be canceled before shipping. The team aims for "all transitions coverage" in addition to testing every correct transition. What else must I do?
options: There is no need to do anything additional because passing every state is considered complete.
There is no need to do anything else because all the correct transition lines are already covered.
Try doing all invalid transitions in one test to save time.
Try doing an incorrect transition, such as canceling it after delivery, by separating the tests.
questions.explain: all transitions coverage covers all valid transitions and must also attempt invalid transitions. Trying one test at a time avoids defect masking, where one defect blocks the other. Combining multiple cases into a single test risks errors. Valid transitions are a weaker level.

questions.prompt: getUser is an async function that should throw "not found" but there is a bug causing it to return null instead, even though the test below is still green. How should I fix the test to catch this bug?
options: Put await in front of expect(e.message) in catch to wait for test results.
Change it to expect(() => getUser(999)).toThrow("not found") without using await.
Change it to await expect(getUser(999)).rejects.toThrow("not found")
Longer the test timeout to give the catch time to work.
questions.explain: When getUser doesn't throw, the code in the catch never runs, so no assertions are called and the test passes without checking. Resolve it with .rejects (if the promise succeeds, the test will fail itself) or add expect.assertions(1). As for adding await in the catch, it doesn't change the fact that the catch doesn't run. And toThrow without await doesn't work with async functions because it returns the promise that rejects instead of immediately throwing it. Even if the code is correct, the test will still fail.

questions.prompt: These two test items are in the same file. Run with test.only only for the second item and it passes. But when running the entire file, the second one fails. What is the cause and the correct solution?
options: Jest runs tests in random order. They should always be set to run in order in the file.
The count function has a bug only when called multiple times. You should only edit the actual code.
Should be changed to beforeAll to create cart once to make it faster than before.
The cart is shared between tests, so it has a stuck state. You should create a new one in beforeEach.
questions.explain: The cart file level is edited by the first test, causing the second test to see the remaining contents. which will not be found when running alone Creating a new beforeEach makes all tests start from the same state. beforeAll makes the state more shared, and Jest doesn't randomize the order of tests in normal files.

questions.prompt: One PR changed a component causing the snapshot test to fail on 14 dev files. Run jest -u and commit all without opening them. What are the problems with this method and what should be done?
options: No problem, because snapshots are created from real code and are always correct.
jest -u approves everything that was not intended, should read the diff first.
You should not commit the .snap file because it is automatically generated by Jest.
You should delete all snapshot tests and rewrite them with toBe.
questions.explain: The .snap file is considered part of the test and must be reviewed like code. Uncommitted updates cause tests to accept unintended behavior changes. Not committing the .snap file is wrong because Jest recommends committing it in version control.

questions.prompt: dev wrote a new test that uses toMatchSnapshot Passed on my own machine but forgot to commit the .snap file, then CI ran Jest with --ci, what will happen?
options: The test passes and Jest automatically writes a new .snap file on the CI.
The test is skipped and is skipped until there is a .snap file in the repo.
test fails because CI doesn't write new snapshots for you, you have to commit the .snap file.
The test passes, but Jest warns that there is a snapshot that has not yet been saved to a file.
questions.explain: In --ci mode, new snapshots are not written if they are not sent. --updateSnapshot and test will fail to automatically prevent snapshots that have never been reviewed. Options that say write files to CI are the opposite of actual behavior.

questions.prompt: The dev wrote this code and Jest complained that the module factory of jest.mock() does not refer to variables outside of scope. Which one correctly describes the cause and solution?
questions.code:
const fakeMailer = { send: jest.fn() };
jest.mock('./mailer', () => fakeMailer);
options: jest.fn cannot be used in factory. You must write a mock function as a normal function.
jest.mock must be moved after require because Jest always runs in line order.
jest.doMock must be used every time factory references an external variable. There's no way around it.
jest.mock is hoisted to the top, so variable names start with mock.
questions.explain: jest.mock is raised to the top of the file. The variables declared below are not yet assigned to Jest, so we'll set them aside for now. Except for names starting with mock , which the author must guarantee is configured in time, jest.doMock is an alternative to hoist, but not the only way.

questions.prompt: This E2E test sometimes passes, sometimes fails because the toast "saved" appears approximately 300 ms after clicking. How should I fix this to get to the root cause?
questions.code:
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'บันทึก' }).click();
expect(await page.getByText('บันทึกแล้ว').isVisible()).toBe(true);
options: Use await expect(page.getByText("Saved")).toBeVisible()
Add await page.waitForTimeout(2000) before the line that checks for toast to wait long enough.
Set the test runner's retries to 3, try rerunning the entire test when it fails.
Changed the locator to be a more specific and more stable CSS selector for toast.
questions.explain: isVisible() checks once and returns the value immediately, without waiting. For web-first assertions like toBeVisible(), it will retry until the condition is true or the timeout expires. A fixed number delay is still guesswork, and the runner's retry just hides the problem.

questions.prompt: The designer refactored the entire website's CSS class name, causing almost the entire E2E set to fail even though the screen works as before. Most locators are written as div.card > button.btn-x1:nth-child(2) . How should I adjust this?
options: Designers are prohibited from changing class names again because tests rely on these names.
Change to getByRole with the agreed upon button name or test id.
Switch to full XPath from root because it's more precise than CSS.
Cut the E2E count in half to reduce refactoring time.
questions.explain: A locator tied to a DOM structure or class will break when the markup structure changes even though the behavior remains the same. Playwright recommends using a locator that is closer to what the user perceives, such as a role or test id as a convention. Long XPaths are more fragile.

questions.prompt: The "Edit Profile" test in E2E depends on the previous "Login" test running successfully and leaving the session intact. When running alone or in parallel, it fails. How should I fix this by allowing each test to run in parallel and being able to tell which features are broken?
options: Force the running order to always test login first. then turn off parallel running
Combine every step into one long test so that you don't have to depend on each other.
Set retry to test profile edits in case the session arrives in time.
Have each test log itself in beforeEach without relying on other tests.
questions.explain: Each test should be independent with its own storage, cookies, and data. This makes the results repeatable and easy to debug. Forcing the sequence solves the problem but causes one test to break and spread to many others. A single, long test, even without relying on other tests, combines so many behaviors that it's impossible to immediately tell which feature is broken.

questions.prompt: This property test always passes even though sortNumbers returns an unsorted array. What property should I add to catch the sorting bug?
options: Check that all pairs of adjacent members are arranged in ascending order.
Increase the number of random rounds tenfold for greater coverage.
Verify that the result is always an array, regardless of the input.
Verify that sortNumbers does not throw on any random input.
questions.explain: The previous property only checked the length, which the implementation Those that are not sorted are passed. You must add a property that directly mentions the order. Adding randomness doesn't help if the property doesn't check for errors. And checking whether it is an array or not, throw is a too weak condition.

questions.prompt: Before the release, there are two days left for testing. There are three parts: a completely rewritten payment module, an About page that only changes the text. and internal reports used once a month How should they be ranked according to the concept of risk-based testing?
options: Start with the part that is easiest to test first in order to get the highest coverage as quickly as possible.
Let's start with the payment module. Because the chance of being wrong and the impact are both high.
Arrange the menus in the app so you don't miss anything.
Allocate the time equally to achieve team equality.
questions.explain: Risk level comes from likelihood and impact. Newly written code has a high chance of being wrong, and mistakes involving money have a high impact. Therefore, you should get the most sequence and time possible. As for starting with the easy part, the coverage numbers are good but do not reduce the actual risk.

questions.prompt: This function has only one test. How will discount(1000, true) coverage report come out? And what must be added to provide complete branch coverage?
options: statement 100% and branch 100% because every line is run in one test.
statement 50% and branch 50% must add a complete test in both cases.
statement 100% but the branch is incomplete, need to add the case isMember to false
The statement is incomplete, you need to add a test through the return line as well.
questions.explain: A single test runs every line (statement 100%) but never goes to the if-false path, so it doesn't reach 100% branch coverage (actually runs 50%). The branch coverage covers the statement coverage, but not vice versa.

questions.prompt: The team got a new file import feature with very thin specs and only one day left before delivery. What type of supplementary testing is most appropriate?
options: Use session-based exploratory testing with a charter and time frame.
Wait until the specs are complete before testing. In order not to waste time testing the wrong thing.
Write detailed, fully documented test cases in advance to complete all cases before starting to run.
Only use unit tests because they run quickly and do not require the tester's discretion.
questions.explain: exploratory testing Design, run, and evaluate tests while learning the system. This is useful when specs are small or time is limited. Having a session with a charter and time box gives structure, while waiting for specs leaves no time to test.

exercises.title: Write a unit test for a delivery value function that covers the margin values.
exercises.prompt: The shippingFee(total) function charges a shipping fee of 50 baht, free shipping when the amount is over 500 baht, and throws an error when the amount is negative. Write a unit test with Jest, at least 4 tests, with each test checking one behavior and calling shippingFee directly to cover the margin values ​​on both sides of 500, the amount 0, and the negative amount.
hints: Separate behavior first: peaks under 500, peaks above 500, and negative peaks, and find values ​​at the edges of each group.
The margins of the free shipping rule are 499 and 500, and the margins of the negative balance rule are -1 and 0.
In the case of an error, it must be wrapped in a function: expect(() => shippingFee(-1)).toThrow() If you write expect(shippingFee(-1)) an error will occur before expect can run.

checks.label: There are at least 4 test cases.
Testing the edge value of 500 is exactly right.
Test under-margin value 499
Test balance 0
Test error cases with toThrow
Don't call throw functions directly in expect.
Check the returned value with toBe or toEqual.

exercises.title: Wrote an async test that uses stub and mock to send welcome email function.
exercises.prompt: The sendWelcome function accepts repo (retrieving users) and mailer (sending email) as dependencies. Write at least 3 async Jest tests: (1) the user has an email address, must return sent true and call mailer.send with the user's email address (2) the user does not have an email address, must return sent false and not call mailer.send (3) the user is not found, must reject with the message user not found, use jest.fn() to create a stub with a mock instead of the real one and await every promise.
hints: The dependency is sent as an argument, so create a fake object and send it in without having to jest.mock the entire module and should create a new one in beforeEach so that the state doesn't get stuck and skip testing.
repo.findById and mailer.send are async, so use jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(...) to return a promise and the test must be async with await sendWelcome(...)

In case you don't have an email address expect(mailer.send).not.toHaveBeenCalled() In case the user is not found, use await expect(sendWelcome(...)).rejects.toThrow("user not found"). If you forget, await test will end before checking.

checks.label: There are at least 3 test cases.
test is async uses await and stub of repo, returns promise (mockResolvedValue, async function or Promise.resolve)
Returns both sent true (with email address) and sent false (without email address).
Verify that mailer.send is called with the user's email address.
Make sure that if there is no email, do not call mailer.send.
If the user is not found, check reject with rejects, expect.assertions or keep the error for checking outside of catch.
Don't forget to await or return in front of expect(...).rejects/resolves

exercises.title: Test retry with delay by controlling the time with fake timers.
exercises.prompt: The retry function calls fn again when rejecting, waiting for delayMs between rounds, and rejecting with the most recent error on every failure. (Initial call 1 time and repeated retries according to the number of retries) The team had an original test that had a real wait time of more than two seconds. Slow and relies on a real clock Let's rewrite it with fake timers without waiting for the real timer at all. Covers (1) succeeding on the 3rd time after two failures, fn is called 3 times, (2) before delayMs fn is still called only 1 time, and a second time when the timer expires, (3) every failure is rejected with the last error, and returning real timers after every test.
hints: Turn on fake timers in beforeEach with jest.useFakeTimers() and return real clocks in afterEach with jest.useRealTimers() to avoid spreading to other tests.

retry waits with a promise between cycles, so use await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(ms) which allows the promise callback to run before the time runs, while sync doesn't let the waiting promise continue running.

In the case of rejecting every round, tie const assertion = expect(retry(...)).rejects.toThrow("...") before delaying, then await the assertion at the end of the test. If delaying before, promise will reject without anyone receiving the error and Jest will report it as unhandled rejection.

checks.label: Turn on fake timers with jest.useFakeTimers()
Advance time with async version (advanceTimersByTimeAsync or runAllTimersAsync)
Returns real timers in afterEach (or afterAll)
Confirm that fn is called only 1 time before the delay completes.
Verify that fn has been called 3 times.
Check for every failure with .rejects.
Don't wait for real time with setTimeout number in test
